title: Block ciphers, stream ciphers and AES
summary: What AES actually does to 16 bytes, how that differs from a stream cipher, and why raw AES is only a building block.

steps.title: Two kinds of cipher
body: A **block cipher** is a keyed scramble of a fixed-size block. AES takes exactly **16 bytes** in and gives exactly 16 bytes out; with the same key, decryption runs the scramble backwards. On its own it cannot encrypt a 17-byte message.
A **stream cipher** produces a long **keystream** from a key and a nonce, and XORs it with the message, exactly like the one-time pad from module 1, but with a short key. ChaCha20 is a stream cipher.
| Works on | 16-byte blocks | any number of bytes |
| Example | AES (also the old DES, 3DES) | ChaCha20 (also the broken RC4) |
| Needs | a **mode** to handle real messages | a **nonce** that never repeats |
A **mode of operation** is the recipe that turns a block cipher into something that encrypts messages. Some modes (CTR, GCM) turn AES into a stream cipher.

steps.explain: AES itself is a block cipher, but CTR mode (and GCM, which is built on CTR) uses it to generate a keystream, so the result behaves like a stream cipher.

steps.title: AES in .NET
body: AES has a 16-byte block and a key of 16, 24 or 32 bytes (AES-128, AES-192, AES-256). The number in the name is the **key** size; the block is always 128 bits.
The raw primitive, one block in and one block out, is `EncryptEcb` with no padding:
byte[] c = aes.EncryptEcb(block, PaddingMode.None);       // 16 bytes in, 16 out
byte[] p = aes.DecryptEcb(c, PaddingMode.None);           // and back
The official test vector (FIPS-197) for AES-256 with key `00 01 02 ... 1f` encrypts `00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff` to `8ea2b7ca516745bfeafc49904b496089`. You will reproduce it in a moment.

> **Fixed values for the exercises only.** The keys, IVs and nonces here are constants so the output is the same every run. Real code takes keys from `RandomNumberGenerator` or a key vault and never repeats a nonce with the same key.

steps.explain: `Aes.Create()` makes a random 256-bit (32-byte) key by default. One block in gives exactly one block out.

steps.prompt: What does the **256** in AES-256 refer to?
options: The largest message it can encrypt
steps.explain: AES always has a 128-bit block. The key can be 128, 192 or 256 bits; AES-256 runs 14 rounds instead of 10.

steps.title: Same key, same block, same output
body: A block cipher is **deterministic**: with one key, a given 16-byte block always encrypts to the same 16 bytes. That is what makes decryption possible, and it is also the reason raw AES is not a safe way to encrypt a message: an attacker can tell when two blocks were equal. The next lesson shows exactly how that leaks.
The other property you want from a good block cipher is the **avalanche effect**: change one input bit and about half of the 128 output bits change, in a pattern nobody can predict without the key.

code: aes.Key = new byte[32];                     // fixed for the demo
steps.explain: Raw AES has no randomness of its own: the same key and block always give the same ciphertext, and decryption inverts it exactly.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: the secret that selects one of the cipher's scrambles
the 16 bytes AES works on at a time
the recipe for encrypting messages longer than one block
a per-message value that makes equal messages encrypt differently
pseudo-random bytes XORed with the message
steps.explain: Only the key is secret. The nonce or IV travels openly next to the ciphertext.

steps.title: Raw AES, one block
prompt: Write `byte[] AesBlock(byte[] key, byte[] block)` that encrypts exactly one 16-byte block with raw AES (`EncryptEcb` with `PaddingMode.None`), and `byte[] AesBlockInverse(byte[] key, byte[] block)` that decrypts one. Both throw `ArgumentException` unless the block is exactly 16 bytes.
The tests check the FIPS-197 vector: key `000102...1f`, plaintext `00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff`, ciphertext `8ea2b7ca516745bfeafc49904b496089`.
solution: if (block.Length != 16) throw new ArgumentException("AES works on exactly 16 bytes.");
if (block.Length != 16) throw new ArgumentException("AES works on exactly 16 bytes.");
template: Dojo.Eq("the inverse gives the block back", dojoPlain, AesBlockInverse(dojoKey, AesBlock(dojoKey, dojoPlain)));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("15 bytes are rejected", () => AesBlock(dojoKey, new byte[15]));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("17 bytes are rejected", () => AesBlockInverse(dojoKey, new byte[17]));

steps.title: Measure the avalanche
prompt: Write `int BitsChanged(byte[] key, byte[] block, int bit)`: encrypt `block`, then encrypt a copy with bit number `bit` flipped (bit `i` is bit `i % 8` of byte `i / 8`, so flip with `copy[bit / 8] ^= (byte)(1 << (bit % 8))`), and return how many of the 128 output bits differ.
Count differing bits with `System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount((uint)(a[i] ^ b[i]))` per byte. A one-bit change in, roughly 64 bits changed out: that is the avalanche.
starter: int BitsChanged(byte[] key, byte[] block, int bit)
solution: int BitsChanged(byte[] key, byte[] block, int bit)
template: int DojoExpected(byte[] k, byte[] blk, int bit)
Dojo.Eq($"BitsChanged with bit {dojoBit} flipped", DojoExpected(dojoKey, dojoBlock, dojoBit), BitsChanged(dojoKey, dojoBlock, dojoBit));
var dojoAll = Enumerable.Range(0, 128).Select(b => BitsChanged(dojoKey, dojoBlock, b)).ToList();
Dojo.Check("on average about half the bits change", dojoAll.Average() is > 56 and < 72, $"average was {dojoAll.Average():F1}");
Dojo.Check("the input block is not modified", System.Text.Encoding.ASCII.GetString(dojoBlock) == "sixteen byte msg", "BitsChanged changed its input");
